governing_job: Change what the reader means when they use the word “prosperity.”
central_proposition: Prosperity is not merely earning more. It is retaining more, owning more, becoming less fragile, gaining greater agency, and having more control over one's time.

five_dimensions.label: Income
five_dimensions.question: What resources come in?
five_dimensions.plain: Wages, salaries, business income, retirement income, ownership income, and transfers that enter the household.

five_dimensions.label: Cost
five_dimensions.question: What must leave just to maintain ordinary life?
five_dimensions.plain: Housing, food, energy, transportation, insurance, childcare, healthcare, taxes, and other essentials/obligations.

five_dimensions.label: Security
five_dimensions.question: Can the household absorb disruption?
five_dimensions.plain: Cash buffers, insurance, debt burden, reliable essentials, portable skills, community capacity — and careful use of credit.

five_dimensions.label: Ownership
five_dimensions.question: What does the household possess that can build future wealth?
five_dimensions.plain: Home equity, retirement assets, business equity, productive investments — diversified enough that one failure doesn't take everything.

five_dimensions.label: Time
five_dimensions.question: How much control does the household have over its own life?
five_dimensions.plain: Predictable hours, commute burden, care load, administrative friction — time as a form of wealth.

not_saying.title: What Constitutional Capitalism is NOT saying
items: Every household should make the same choices
People should be prevented from becoming wealthy
instead: The purpose of the economic system is broader than producing transactions.
The household — not the statistic — is where prosperity ultimately has to become real.

stage4_preservations: Demand-side housing without supply can be captured (4.3)
Worker ownership is not universally beneficial without risk disclosure (4.3)
Retraining is not a universal AI fix (4.4)
No magic single prosperity score — panel required (4.5)

sections.heading: They make more money than their parents did. So why don't they feel richer?
prose: Return to the Rivers household.
Give them a raise. Household income rises. On a spreadsheet, that looks like progress.

Then housing costs more. Insurance costs more. Groceries cost more. The vehicle costs more. Childcare consumes income. Healthcare creates uncertainty. Debt payments continue. Every unexpected $1,000 expense threatens the monthly budget.
On paper: Income ↑.
Did their prosperity increase?
Maybe. Maybe not.
That question is the doorway into this chapter — and into Constitutional Capitalism.

sections.heading: The scoreboard we've been using is incomplete
prose: Income matters. But $70,000 in one place or period does not buy what $70,000 buys somewhere else.
GDP matters. It tells us something about economic production. GDP can still rise while particular households become less secure.

Jobs are essential. But 'a job exists' does not tell us what it pays, whether benefits exist, whether hours are predictable, whether the worker can build assets, or whether the job survives the next technological change.
Government revenue is necessary for government. A government becoming richer by extracting more from increasingly fragile households is not our definition of prosperity.
Economic activity is not the same thing as human prosperity.

sections.heading: The Household Prosperity Dashboard
prose: Constitutional Capitalism measures households across five dimensions — not one slogan.
Income: What resources come in?
Cost: What must leave just to maintain ordinary life?
Security: Can the household absorb disruption?
Ownership: What does the household possess that can build future wealth?
Time: How much control does the household have over its own life?
Keep returning to these five. Everything else in this chapter orbits them.

sections.heading: Income — the beginning, not the destination
prose: Income includes wages and salaries, business income, retirement income, investment or ownership income, and transfers that lawfully enter the household.
Gross income is not disposable income. Disposable income is not Prosperity Surplus.
A household can earn more while retaining less.
That is the key. Income starts the story. It does not end it.

sections.heading: Cost — prosperity has a denominator
prose: A $5,000 raise does not create $5,000 of prosperity if rent rises $2,000, insurance rises $1,000, food rises $800, and transportation rises $700.

Stage 4 forced this confrontation. Demand-side assistance can sometimes be captured by constrained markets. More money chasing the same number of houses can raise housing prices. Greater healthcare access without healthcare capacity can create waiting rather than care.
We cannot measure what government gives people without measuring what the systems around them take back.
For the Rivers household, the raise and the grocery bill arrive in the same week. Prosperity lives in that collision.

sections.heading: Prosperity Surplus
prose: Prosperity Surplus = Resources − Essentials − Obligations.
It is not 'money left over for luxuries.'
It is the household's room to save, invest, repair the roof, replace a vehicle, survive unemployment, start a business, care for family, take a class, reduce debt, or simply breathe financially.
Evidence discipline, stated plainly: we do not currently claim to know one statewide Arkansas Prosperity Surplus number.
We built the measurement architecture. We did not fabricate the answer. Unknown is honest. A fake statewide total is not.

sections.heading: Security — what happens when Tuesday goes wrong?
prose: The transmission fails. Someone misses work. The roof leaks. A child gets sick. Hours are cut. A storm damages the house.
Prosperity is not merely how well the household performs during an ordinary month. It includes: How far can life move away from normal before the household begins to collapse?
Household resilience includes cash reserves, insurance, debt burden, reliable essential services, portable skills, and family or community capacity.
Access to credit can help absorb a shock. Stage 4 also killed a dangerous slogan: credit is not prosperity. Credit can turn today's emergency into years of payments.
Security asks whether the Rivers household can survive Tuesday — not only whether Friday's paycheck cleared.

sections.heading: Ownership — the difference between earning and accumulating
prose: Two households earn the same amount. One owns home equity, retirement assets, business equity, productive investments. The other owns almost nothing and rents or finances nearly everything it uses.
Their incomes can be identical. Their economic positions are not.
Income pays for today. Ownership can carry value into tomorrow.

Do not romanticize ownership. Stage 4 taught us ownership can concentrate risk. A worker whose paycheck, retirement, and company stock all depend on one employer may technically own more while becoming less diversified.

The goal is not ownership at any cost. It is durable, appropriately diversified household capital formation — building stakes in the future without betting the whole family's tomorrow on a single failure.

sections.heading: Time — the forgotten form of wealth
prose: Consider two people earning $60,000. One works predictable hours ten minutes from home. The other works unpredictable shifts, drives ninety minutes, juggles childcare, and spends evenings navigating bills and services.
Same income. Very different lives.
Who is wealthier in control over their own existence?
Time is not merely leisure. Time enables parenting, education, civic participation, caregiving, entrepreneurship, relationships, rest, volunteering, and community.
A political-economic system that increases income while consuming every waking hour has achieved something — but not everything Constitutional Capitalism means by prosperity.

sections.heading: Agency ties the five together
prose: Income plus manageable costs plus security plus ownership plus time produce something larger: agency.
Agency is the ability to make meaningful choices without every decision being dictated by immediate economic survival.
Agency does not mean government guarantees every desired outcome. It means prosperity gives people room to choose.
That is where economic liberty meets constitutional liberty — not as slogan, but as lived capacity.

sections.heading: Three Rivers households
prose: Hold the same family in three hypothetical conditions. All scenes are ILLUSTRATION — teaching tools, not Arkansas statistics.
Rivers A — Higher Income, Higher Pressure: income rises substantially; costs and debt rise almost as quickly; little savings; no meaningful ownership increase; less time.
Rivers B — Lower Headline Income, Greater Security: slightly lower income; lower essential costs; emergency savings; some retirement assets; predictable work; more time.
Rivers C — Compounding Prosperity: income grows; essential-cost burden stabilizes; debt declines; assets accumulate; skills increase; time control improves.
Which household is actually becoming prosperous?
Do not answer with income alone. Let the five dimensions answer.

sections.heading: Geography changes the equation
prose: Bring Phillips County back in — carefully, with facts.

A dollar does not encounter the same economic environment everywhere. Rural households may face long transportation distances, limited healthcare access, fewer childcare providers, thin labor markets, limited broadband. Urban and suburban households may face higher housing costs, congestion, different childcare pressures, land scarcity.
The point is not that one is always worse. Prosperity has geography.

Statewide medians can hide that. Chapter 1 showed Phillips County's population loss and elevated poverty beside Arkansas' statewide median. This chapter insists the prosperity dashboard must be able to see place — preparing Geographic Money Statements and productive systems later.

sections.heading: Disability and accessibility belong inside economics
prose: Do not leave accessibility buried in technical appendices.

A system can report jobs, wages, and growth while being practically inaccessible to part of the population. Transportation, housing design, workplace access, healthcare, digital services, care requirements, and administrative complexity can all impose economic costs.
Accessibility is not a sidebar to prosperity. It changes the household ledger itself — what income can buy, what time is consumed, what security costs, and what ownership is reachable.

sections.heading: From household to community
prose: One prosperous household cannot sustain a hospital, a grocery store, a school, a bank, a water system, local businesses, or community institutions alone.
Households interact. Their spending becomes business revenue. Businesses create income. Ownership produces capital. Taxes finance public systems. Community capacity changes household opportunity.
Household → Community → Productive Systems → Household.
That loop prepares the rest of the book — especially Follow the Money and The Productive Arkansas.

sections.heading: Intergenerational prosperity
prose: Imagine the Rivers children twenty-five years from now. What did they inherit?
Not merely money. Infrastructure, schools, public debt, natural resources, institutions, housing stock, productive businesses, technology, community capacity, and political institutions.
A generation is not prosperous if its standard of living depends on consuming the productive inheritance of the generation after it.
Stage 4 also locked the balance: we cannot hoard resources for hypothetical future people while current children suffer legitimate necessities.
Prosperity must serve present capability and future capability — together.

sections.heading: Then — the definition
prose: Only after living through income, cost, surplus, security, ownership, time, agency, place, accessibility, community, and inheritance does the locked definition mean what it should:
Prosperity is not merely earning more. It is retaining more, owning more, becoming less fragile, gaining greater agency, and having more control over one's time.
Now it means something.

The next chapter follows the money — why two places can produce similar activity yet accumulate radically different wealth, and how ownership, capital, leakage, and Arkansas' money system connect to the household dashboard you just learned.
